Heat and the Brain: Extreme Heat Exposure vs. Neurological Care Access in North and East Texas

Independent research project. Updated 2026-11-18 with 24 counties, 1,885 Census tracts, and verified medical sources.

Executive Summary

Research question. Across North and East Texas, which rural counties combine high extreme-heat exposure with limited access to emergency and neurological care, and which patient groups face the highest risk?

Approach. Twenty-four counties (4 urban DFW core counties and 20 surrounding rural/exurban counties) were evaluated on seven public-data measures: extreme-heat days (≥100°F/yr, 2015–2024), % residents age 65+, % households with no vehicle, stroke prevalence, neurologists per 100,000, population-weighted driving time to the nearest ER, and population-weighted driving time to the nearest neurology hub (an ER hospital in a county with ≥10 neurologists). Measures were ranked 1–24, averaged into Heat, Vulnerability, and Access gap, and combined with equal weights.

  • Hill County ranks highest (19.89 of 24), scoring near 20 across all three dimensions: 19.4 heat days/yr, 20.3% age 65+, 6.2% no-vehicle households, 0 neurologists, 22.3 min average ER drive, and 70.8 min average neurology-hub drive.
  • Top 5 counties overall: Hill (19.89), Erath (16.83), Navarro (16.72), Hood (16.22 — hottest at 34.2 days ≥100°F), and Hunt (14.78).
  • Rural vs. urban access gap: Rural residents drive an average of 19.3 minutes to the nearest ER vs. 9.1 minutes in the urban core, and 50.7 minutes to a neurology hub vs. 9.1 minutes in the urban core.
  • Neurologist deserts: 12 of the 20 rural counties have 0 neurologists on record (HRSA AHRF 2023).

1. Project Flow

Public climate, Census, health, and hospital datasets feed a reproducible Python pipeline that routes 1,885 Census tracts and generates the risk score, interactive map, and this report.

2. Background (Verified Sources)

  • How heat affects neurological conditions: Extreme heat, dehydration, and overheating lower seizure thresholds, trigger migraines, temporarily worsen multiple sclerosis symptoms (Uhthoff's phenomenon), strain cardiovascular and stroke recovery, and increase overheating and wandering risks in dementia and Parkinson's disease (see Table C).
  • Medications that affect temperature regulation: The CDC reports that diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, stimulants, and tricyclic antidepressants can blunt thirst, alter sweating, or impair central thermoregulation, and ambient heat can degrade temperature-sensitive medicines. Patients should review heat-medication plans with a clinician and never stop prescriptions abruptly (CDC Heat and Medications Guidance, cdc.gov/heat-health/hcp/clinical-guidance/heat-and-medications-guidance-for-clinicians.html).
  • Why older adults (65+) and rural residents face higher risk: Adults 65+ have reduced sweat response and temperature awareness and more chronic conditions (CDC Heat and Older Adults, cdc.gov/heat-health/risk-factors/heat-and-older-adults-aged-65.html). In rural counties, limited public transit (no-vehicle households) and longer travel times to emergency and neurology care compound these biological risks.

Key Peer-Reviewed & Aging-Research Studies

  • Outdoor extreme heat & dementia disparities (20-year U.S. study, Alzheimer's & Dementia; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13688717/): Exposure to "Danger+" heat days (heat index ≥103°F) was linked to higher dementia incidence, with steeper risks in neighborhoods with lower air-conditioning prevalence and greater socioeconomic disadvantage.
  • Cumulative extreme heat & cognitive decline (Choi, Lee, & Chang, J. Epidemiol. Community Health 2023, 77(11):728–735; doi:10.1136/jech-2023-220675): Analyzing Health and Retirement Study data (2006–2018, adults 52+), cumulative heat exposure was associated with faster cognitive decline among Black older adults and residents of lower-income neighborhoods.
  • Home temperature & cognitive function in older adults (Baniassadi, Hebrew SeniorLife / Marcus Institute for Aging Research, 2025; hebrewseniorlife.org/blog/how-home-temperature-affects-cognitive-function-older-adults): Explains how real-world indoor home temperatures affect attention and cognition in older adults and why cost/housing barriers make staying cool harder.

6. Discussion & Recommendations (Hypotheses for Further Action)

  • Telehealth neurology expansion in the 12 rural counties with zero neurologists, prioritizing high-heat/high-vulnerability counties like Hill, Erath, and Navarro.
  • Older-adult heat & medication check-ins in counties with >20% residents age 65+ (Hood 25.4%, Rains 24.2%, Henderson 22.4%, Hill 20.3%, Van Zandt 20.2%).
  • EMS & cooling-center planning in long-ER-drive counties such as Van Zandt (42.3 min avg ER drive) and Rains (33.1 min).

7. Limitations

  • Ecological county-level analysis shows association, not causation.
  • One NOAA weather station represents each county; local urban heat islands or microclimates are not captured.
  • Neurology hubs are approximated as ER hospitals in counties with ≥10 neurologists (HRSA AHRF 2023); satellite clinics and out-of-state hubs are not included.
  • Equal group weights are a methodological choice; rank scores show relative ordering rather than absolute clinical risk.

Informational only. Not medical advice. In an emergency, call 911.
